question: What is the difference between REST and SOAP?
title: REST vs SOAP
direct_answer: REST is an architectural style using HTTP with JSON/XML, emphasizing simplicity and statelessness. SOAP is a protocol with strict XML-based messaging, built-in error handling (WSDL/SOAP faults), and enterprise features like WS-Security. REST dominates modern web APIs; SOAP persists in enterprise/banking systems.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of different API paradigms and ability to choose the right one
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying SOAP is just old REST or not knowing when SOAP is still appropriate
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that SOAP has advantages in transaction management, security, and ACID compliance

sections.title: REST vs SOAP: Two Approaches to APIs
sections.content:
Both REST and SOAP are ways to build APIs, but they solve the problem differently. **REST (Representational State Transfer)** is an architectural style that treats everything as a resource (users, orders, products) accessible via standard HTTP methods. You call GET /users/123 and get back JSON.

It's lightweight and aligns naturally with how the web works. **SOAP (Simple Object Access Protocol)** is a protocol with strict rules: everything is XML, every request has a SOAP envelope, and the server publishes a WSDL (Web Services Description Language) file describing exactly what operations are available. Think of REST like ordering food at a counter (simple, flexible) and SOAP like filling out a government form (rigid, but with guarantees). SOAP dominated the 2000s for enterprise integration; REST took over in the 2010s for web and mobile APIs because it's easier to use and debug.

sections.title: When to Choose Each
sections.content:
Use **REST** when building modern web or mobile APIs, when you need simplicity and wide client compatibility, or when your data model maps naturally to resources. It's the default choice for startups and consumer-facing applications.

Use **SOAP** when you need guaranteed delivery with ACID transactions, when working with legacy enterprise systems (banking, insurance, telecom), when WS-Security's encryption and signature standards are required, or when you need formal contracts enforced by WSDL. Financial institutions still use SOAP for payment processing because the built-in transaction support and security are battle-tested.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming SOAP is obsolete**: Freshers dismiss SOAP as old technology, but it's still used in banking, healthcare, and government systems where formal contracts and transaction guarantees matter. Not knowing this makes you look unaware of enterprise realities.
- **Not understanding REST's limitations**: REST has no built-in transaction support or distributed transaction coordination. If you need ACID guarantees across services, REST alone won't give you that.
- **Confusing protocol with transport**: SOAP can run over HTTP, but also SMTP or message queues. REST is tied to HTTP. This matters when designing integration with non-HTTP systems.

sections.title: Spring Boot Example
Key Points
content: **Architectural style vs protocol**: REST is a design philosophy using HTTP; SOAP is a formal protocol with XML envelopes and strict rules
**JSON vs XML**: REST commonly uses JSON (lighter, easier to parse); SOAP mandates XML with schema validation
**WSDL contract**: SOAP requires a WSDL file that acts like a typed interface definition; REST has optional OpenAPI specs
**Built-in security**: SOAP includes WS-Security for message-level encryption and signing; REST relies on transport-level HTTPS and tokens
**Error handling**: REST uses HTTP status codes (404, 500); SOAP wraps errors in SOAP Fault elements with detailed codes
**Statelessness**: REST enforces stateless interactions; SOAP can maintain conversational state across requests
**Tooling**: SOAP has mature enterprise tooling (SOAPUI, WSDL generators); REST has Postman, Swagger UI, and simpler debugging

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: So REST and SOAP are two different ways to build APIs. REST is an architectural style that uses HTTP naturally. You work with resources like users or orders, and you use GET to read, POST to create, PUT to update. The response is usually JSON, which is lightweight and easy to work with. SOAP is a protocol, meaning it has strict rules. Everything is wrapped in XML, and you need a WSDL file that describes exactly what operations the service offers. It's more heavyweight but gives you built-in features like WS-Security for encryption and signing, and better support for transactions. In my understanding, REST won because it's simpler. If you're building a mobile app or a public API, REST is the obvious choice. But SOAP is still alive in banking and enterprise systems. For example, payment gateways often use SOAP because they need the transaction guarantees and formal contracts. One thing freshers miss is assuming SOAP is just old tech. It's not. It's still the right choice when you need ACID transactions across services or when you're integrating with legacy enterprise systems that demand WS-Security standards. Knowing when each fits shows you understand real-world trade-offs, not just the latest trends.

question: What is GraphQL and how does it compare to REST?
title: GraphQL vs REST
direct_answer: GraphQL is a query language for APIs where clients specify exactly what data they need. Unlike REST (multiple endpoints, fixed response shape), GraphQL has one endpoint and returns exactly what's requested — no over-fetching or under-fetching.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of modern API alternatives and their tradeoffs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying GraphQL is always better — it has real downsides (complexity, caching difficulty)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention N+1 problem in GraphQL and data loader pattern

sections.title: GraphQL: Client-Driven Data Fetching
sections.content:
**GraphQL** is a query language created by Facebook to solve a specific problem: mobile apps making too many REST calls or getting too much data back. With REST, you might call GET /users/123, then GET /users/123/orders, then GET /orders/456/items — three round trips.

And each response has a fixed shape, so you get fields you don't need. GraphQL flips this: the client sends a single query describing exactly what it wants, and the server returns only that data. Think of REST like ordering a set menu (you get fries even if you don't want them), and GraphQL like ordering à la carte (you pick exactly what goes on your plate). Instead of multiple endpoints (/users, /orders, /products), GraphQL has one endpoint (usually /graphql) that accepts queries and mutations. This reduces network requests and payload size, which is huge for mobile apps on slow connections.

sections.title: When to Choose Each
sections.content:
Use **GraphQL** when you have complex, nested data relationships (users → orders → items), when mobile clients need to minimize bandwidth and round trips, when different clients need different subsets of data, or when rapid UI iteration requires flexible data fetching without backend changes. It shines in mobile apps and dashboards with many widgets.

Use **REST** when your API is simple with clear resource boundaries, when you need standard HTTP caching (CDNs, browser cache), when the team is unfamiliar with GraphQL's complexity, or when you're building public APIs where simplicity matters. REST is still the default for most CRUD applications. If you have a simple e-commerce backend with products and orders, REST is easier to implement and reason about than GraphQL.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking GraphQL is always better**: Freshers hear about GraphQL solving over-fetching and assume it's superior. But it's harder to implement, harder to cache, and overkill for simple APIs. It's a trade-off, not an upgrade.
- **Ignoring the N+1 query problem**: If your GraphQL resolver naively fetches related data, you can trigger hundreds of database queries for one GraphQL query. This is the infamous N+1 problem. The solution is the DataLoader pattern, which batches and caches requests. Not mentioning this shows you haven't thought about performance.
- **Not understanding caching difficulty**: REST benefits from HTTP caching (ETags, Cache-Control). GraphQL responses are harder to cache because every query can be different, requiring application-level caching strategies like Apollo Client's normalized cache.

sections.title: Spring Boot Example
Key Points
content: **Query language**: GraphQL lets clients write queries specifying fields and nested relations; the server returns exactly that structure
**Single endpoint**: Unlike REST's many endpoints, GraphQL uses one endpoint (typically /graphql) for all queries and mutations
**No over-fetching**: Clients request only the fields they need, reducing payload size and bandwidth usage
**N+1 problem**: Naive GraphQL resolvers can trigger excessive database queries; DataLoader pattern batches and caches requests to solve this
**Schema and types**: GraphQL requires a strongly-typed schema defining all types and operations, providing auto-generated documentation
**Harder caching**: HTTP caching doesn't work well with POST-based GraphQL queries; requires custom or client-side caching strategies
**Mutations and subscriptions**: GraphQL supports mutations (write operations) and subscriptions (real-time updates via WebSockets)

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: GraphQL is a query language for APIs that gives clients control over the data they get back. With REST, you call different endpoints like GET /users/123 and GET /users/123/orders, and each response has a fixed shape. You might get 20 fields when you only need 3. GraphQL changes that. You write a query saying exactly what you want, like asking for a user's name and their last five orders with just item names. The server sends back precisely that, nothing more. It's all done in one request to a single endpoint, usually /graphql. This is amazing for mobile apps where bandwidth matters. Instead of three REST calls, you make one GraphQL query that gets everything. But it's not always better. GraphQL is harder to set up and harder to cache. HTTP caching doesn't work as well because every query can be different. There's also the N+1 problem. If you're not careful, one GraphQL query can trigger hundreds of database queries. You solve that with a DataLoader, which batches requests together. The key is knowing when to use it. If you have a complex app with lots of nested data and multiple client types, GraphQL saves you time. If you have a simple CRUD API, REST is easier and probably better. It's about the right tool for the job.

question: What is gRPC and when would you use it instead of REST?
title: gRPC vs REST
direct_answer: gRPC is a high-performance RPC framework using Protocol Buffers (binary format) over HTTP/2. It's faster than REST/JSON for inter-service communication. Use gRPC for internal microservice communication; use REST for public APIs.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of the API landscape beyond REST
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying gRPC is better in all cases — it's not suitable for browser clients
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that gRPC uses HTTP/2 and supports streaming

sections.title: gRPC: High-Performance Remote Procedure Calls
sections.content:
**gRPC** is a modern RPC (Remote Procedure Call) framework developed by Google for high-performance communication between services. Unlike REST, which uses JSON text over HTTP/1.1, gRPC uses **Protocol Buffers** (a binary serialization format) over **HTTP/2**.

Binary is more compact and faster to parse than JSON. HTTP/2 supports multiplexing (many requests on one connection) and streaming. Think of REST like sending letters (JSON text, slower) and gRPC like sending compressed data packets (binary, faster). In gRPC, you define service methods in a .proto file (like an interface), and the tooling generates client and server code for you. Instead of endpoints like GET /users/123, you call a method like userService.GetUser(id). gRPC is built for service-to-service communication in microservices architectures, where performance and type safety matter more than human readability.

emerald|Streaming|~gRPC natively supports four streaming modes — unary (one request, one response), server stre...
violet|Code generation|~You define services in .proto files, and gRPC generates type-safe client and server code for...

cyan|No browser support|~Browsers don't natively support HTTP/2 request framing for gRPC; you need gRPC-Web and a proxy

sections.title: When to Choose Each
sections.content:
Use **gRPC** when building internal microservices that need low latency and high throughput, when you need bidirectional streaming (like chat or real-time updates), when type safety and contract enforcement matter (Protocol Buffers are strongly typed), or when you're working in a polyglot environment (gRPC generates code for Java, Go, Python, etc.). Netflix and Uber use gRPC internally for service mesh communication.

Use **REST** when building public APIs consumed by third parties or browsers, when you need human-readable debugging (JSON is easy to inspect), when the ecosystem is HTTP/1.1 without HTTP/2 support, or when simplicity trumps performance. REST is still the standard for customer-facing APIs because it's universally supported and easier to work with.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking gRPC works everywhere**: Freshers hear about gRPC's speed and assume it replaces REST. But browsers don't natively support gRPC. You need gRPC-Web and a proxy (like Envoy) to make it work in a browser, which adds complexity. For public APIs, REST is still king.
- **Not understanding the HTTP/2 requirement**: gRPC requires HTTP/2. If your infrastructure doesn't support it (older proxies, some load balancers), gRPC won't work. This is less of an issue with modern cloud platforms, but it's not a drop-in replacement.
- **Ignoring debugging difficulty**: Binary Protocol Buffers aren't human-readable. You can't just curl a gRPC endpoint and see JSON. You need tools like grpcurl or Postman's gRPC support. This makes debugging harder, especially for freshers used to REST.

sections.title: Spring Boot Example
Key Points
content: **Protocol Buffers**: gRPC uses Protobuf, a binary serialization format that's smaller and faster than JSON
**HTTP/2**: gRPC requires HTTP/2, enabling multiplexing (many requests on one connection) and header compression
**Streaming**: gRPC natively supports four streaming modes — unary (one request, one response), server streaming, client streaming, bidirectional streaming
**Code generation**: You define services in .proto files, and gRPC generates type-safe client and server code for multiple languages
**Performance**: Serialization and deserialization are faster than REST/JSON, making gRPC ideal for high-throughput internal APIs
**No browser support**: Browsers don't natively support HTTP/2 request framing for gRPC; you need gRPC-Web and a proxy
**Service mesh integration**: gRPC is commonly used with service mesh tools like Istio and Envoy for microservices observability and routing

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: gRPC is a framework for remote procedure calls that's designed for performance. Instead of JSON over HTTP like REST, it uses Protocol Buffers, which is a binary format, and it runs over HTTP/2. Binary is smaller and faster to parse than JSON text. HTTP/2 lets you send multiple requests over one connection, which is more efficient than REST's typical HTTP/1.1. You define your API in a .proto file that describes the service methods and the request and response types. The gRPC tooling generates client and server code for you in Java, Go, Python, whatever you need. It's strongly typed, so you catch errors at compile time. One big advantage is streaming. gRPC supports bidirectional streaming out of the box. So if you're building a chat service or real-time notifications, gRPC handles that natively. REST doesn't have that. But gRPC isn't for everything. Browsers don't support it natively. You'd need gRPC-Web and a proxy like Envoy, which adds complexity. For public APIs, REST is still the better choice because it's simple and universally supported. Use gRPC for internal microservices where performance matters. That's where it shines. Uber and Netflix use it internally for service-to-service communication. Mentioning that HTTP/2 is required and that gRPC has streaming modes shows you understand the details, not just the hype.

That internal call uses gRPC — binary Protobuf over HTTP/2, 5-10x faster than JSON for high-frequency internal traffic. The client never sees gRPC. In Spring Boot you can expose both: @RestController for the public REST endpoints and a gRPC server via grpc-spring-boot-starter for internal calls. non-obvious: gRPC doesn't work directly from a browser without a grpc-web translation proxy. This is why public APIs always use REST — not because REST is faster.

speakable_v2.cap: REST = JSON + HTTP/1.1 + browser-friendly. gRPC = Protobuf + HTTP/2 + fast internal calls. Use REST for public; gRPC for internal performance-sensitive microservice calls.

question: What is the difference between REST and RPC (Remote Procedure Call)?
title: REST vs RPC
direct_answer: REST focuses on resources and uses HTTP verbs to operate on them (GET /users). RPC focuses on actions — you call remote functions (getUser(), createOrder()). REST is noun-centric, RPC is verb-centric.

interviewer_intent.testing: Conceptual understanding of different API styles
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that many 'REST' APIs are actually more RPC-style
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Recognize that REST's resource model is often violated in practice

sections.title: REST vs RPC: Resources vs Actions
sections.content:
**REST** and **RPC** are two philosophies for designing APIs. REST (Representational State Transfer) models everything as a **resource** (a noun) and uses standard HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) to operate on those resources. You say GET /users/123 to retrieve a user. **RPC (Remote Procedure Call)** models everything as an **action** (a verb). You call a remote function like getUser(123) or createOrder(orderData), treating the API like a library of functions. Think of REST like organizing a library by categories (fiction, science, history) and RPC like asking a librarian to do tasks ("find me a book", "check out this book"). REST emphasizes the what (the resource); RPC emphasizes the how (the operation).

In practice, many APIs labeled REST are actually RPC-style because they have endpoints like POST /orders/123/cancel or POST /users/login, which are action-oriented, not resource-oriented. Pure REST is rare in real-world applications.

sections.title: When to Choose Each
sections.content:
Use **REST** when your domain maps cleanly to resources (users, products, orders) and you want to leverage HTTP caching and semantics. REST is ideal for CRUD operations on entities, public APIs where discoverability matters, and when you want standard HTTP tooling to work out of the box.

Use **RPC** when your API is inherently action-oriented ("send an email", "process payment", "generate report"), when you're building internal service communication where function calls feel natural, or when you need complex operations that don't map to CRUD. Modern RPC frameworks like gRPC are great for microservices. In reality, most APIs are hybrids. You might use REST-style GET /users for reading, but POST /orders/123/refund for actions that don't fit the resource model. Acknowledging this reality shows pragmatism.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking REST is always better**: Freshers are taught REST in courses and assume it's the one true way. But forcing every operation into resource semantics leads to awkward endpoints like POST /users/123/activate. Sometimes an RPC-style endpoint like POST /activateUser is clearer.
- **Not recognizing RPC in the wild**: Many APIs called REST are actually RPC-style. Endpoints like POST /calculate or POST /sendEmail are actions, not resources. Not realizing this shows a shallow understanding of API design.
- **Ignoring HTTP semantics in REST**: REST expects GET to be idempotent and cacheable, POST for creates, PUT for updates, DELETE for deletions. If you're using POST for everything (like RPC does), you're not doing REST, and you lose HTTP caching benefits. Knowing this distinction matters in interviews.

sections.title: Spring Boot Example
Key Points
content: **Resource-centric vs action-centric**: REST treats things as resources (nouns) accessed via HTTP verbs; RPC treats things as functions (verbs) you call remotely
**HTTP verb semantics**: REST uses GET for reads, POST for creates, PUT/PATCH for updates, DELETE for deletes; RPC often uses POST for all operations
**Endpoint naming**: REST uses noun-based paths like /users/123; RPC uses verb-based paths like /getUser or /createOrder
**Caching**: REST leverages HTTP caching naturally (GET responses can be cached); RPC-style POST requests are harder to cache
**HATEOAS**: REST (in theory) includes links to related resources in responses for discoverability; RPC doesn't have this concept
**Real-world APIs**: Many APIs labeled REST are actually RPC-style hybrids because pure REST constraints are hard to maintain for complex domains
**Modern RPC**: Frameworks like gRPC formalize RPC with type safety and code generation, making RPC appealing for microservices

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: REST and RPC are two different ways to think about APIs. REST is resource-centric. You model your API around resources like users, orders, products. You use HTTP verbs to operate on them. So GET /users/123 retrieves a user, POST /users creates a new user, DELETE /users/123 removes one. It's all about the nouns. RPC is action-centric. You're calling remote functions, like getUser or createOrder. It's about the verbs, the operations you're performing. Instead of GET /users/123, you might POST to /getUser with the user ID in the body. REST feels more aligned with how HTTP was designed, so you get benefits like caching for free with GET requests. RPC treats the API more like a library of functions, which can feel more natural for complex business operations. Here's the thing freshers miss: most real-world REST APIs aren't pure REST. You'll see endpoints like POST /orders/123/cancel or POST /sendEmail. Those are actions, not resources. That's RPC-style. And that's fine. Pure REST is hard to maintain when your domain has complex workflows that don't map to CRUD. Knowing this shows you've thought beyond textbook definitions. If an interviewer asks when to use each, say REST for CRUD on entities, RPC for action-heavy operations or internal microservices, and admit that most production APIs are pragmatic hybrids. That's the real-world answer.

followup_questions: How do you model complex actions in REST?

speakable_v2.hook: REST thinks in nouns, RPC thinks in verbs — that one mental shift explains most of the difference.

groups.label: REST
groups.text: Resource-centric. Everything is a noun — /tasks, /users, /orders. You act on resources using HTTP methods as verbs. POST /tasks creates a task. DELETE /tasks/42 removes it.

groups.label: RPC

items: REST for data-centric CRUD: creating, reading, updating, deleting entities maps naturally to resources
RPC (or RPC-style) for complex workflows: /orders/123/approve, /accounts/transfer — actions that don't map cleanly to a single resource and HTTP verb

beats.text: Task app pure REST: POST /tasks (create), GET /tasks/42 (read), PATCH /tasks/42 (update), DELETE /tasks/42 (remove). RPC-style would be: POST /createTask, POST /getTask, POST /updateTask, POST /deleteTask — all POSTs with action names in the URL. In practice many APIs are hybrid: GET /tasks is REST but POST /tasks/42/complete is RPC-style. PATCH /tasks/42 with {done: true} is the REST-pure equivalent. non-obvious: gRPC is a specific RPC implementation. The acronym literally means gRPC Remote Procedure Call.

speakable_v2.cap: REST = nouns + HTTP verbs. RPC = function calls. Real-world APIs often blend both. PATCH /resource with a state change is more RESTful than POST /doAction.

question: How do you choose between REST, GraphQL, gRPC, and WebSocket for your API?
title: Choosing the Right API Technology
direct_answer: Choose REST for standard CRUD and public APIs where simplicity matters. Use GraphQL when clients need flexible data shapes and you want to avoid over-fetching. Pick gRPC for internal microservices requiring high throughput and strict contracts. Use WebSocket for real-time bidirectional communication like chat or live dashboards.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of API protocol tradeoffs and ability to match technology to business requirements rather than following trends.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Choosing based on popularity or resume-building rather than analyzing the actual data access patterns and client needs.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention specific decision factors like network latency constraints, client diversity, and whether the communication pattern is request-response or streaming.

sections.title: Understanding API Protocol Selection
sections.content:
The choice between **REST**, **GraphQL**, **gRPC**, and **WebSocket** depends on three core factors: your **communication pattern** (request-response vs streaming), your **client diversity** (web browsers, mobile apps, internal services), and your **performance requirements** (latency, throughput, payload size). REST dominates public APIs because it's simple, stateless, and works everywhere.

GraphQL emerged to solve the **over-fetching** problem where mobile clients waste bandwidth downloading fields they don't need. gRPC optimizes for speed using **binary serialization** (Protocol Buffers) instead of JSON text, making it ideal for backend-to-backend calls. WebSocket breaks the request-response model entirely, maintaining an **open bidirectional connection** so servers can push data to clients instantly. Think of REST as standard mail, GraphQL as a custom order form, gRPC as an express courier between warehouses, and WebSocket as a phone call that stays connected.

sections.title: Step 1: Analyze Your Communication Pattern
sections.content: Start by identifying whether your communication is **request-response** (client asks, server answers once) or **streaming** (ongoing data flow). For example, a shopping cart checkout is request-response—the client sends order details and gets back a confirmation. Use REST or GraphQL here. A stock trading dashboard showing live prices is streaming—the server continuously pushes updates. Use WebSocket here. If you're building microservices that call each other thousands of times per second (like an order service calling inventory service), that's high-frequency request-response—use gRPC. The Spring Boot default is REST because most CRUD operations (Create, Read, Update, Delete) fit the request-response pattern perfectly.

sections.title: Step 2: Consider Client Type and Data Flexibility Needs
sections.content: Evaluate who consumes your API. **Public APIs** for third-party developers should use REST because it's universally understood and works in any HTTP client. **Mobile apps** with limited bandwidth benefit from GraphQL—they can request exactly the fields they need (userId and userName only, skipping address and preferences). **Internal microservices** in your data center should use gRPC for speed—you control both ends, so binary protocols are fine. If you have an iOS app, Android app, and web dashboard all consuming the same backend but needing different data shapes, GraphQL prevents you from creating three separate REST endpoints. For real-time features like notifications or collaborative editing where the server must **push** data without the client asking, WebSocket is the only practical choice.

sections.title: Step 3: Evaluate Performance and Infrastructure Constraints
sections.content: REST works everywhere because it's just HTTP, but JSON parsing and text serialization add overhead. gRPC reduces payload size by 30-50% using Protocol Buffers and is 5-10x faster for high-throughput scenarios, but requires HTTP/2 support and isn't browser-friendly without a proxy. GraphQL adds server complexity—you need a schema, resolver functions, and protection against expensive nested queries (the **N+1 problem**). WebSocket requires **stateful connections**, meaning your server must hold open sockets for every connected client, limiting horizontal scaling unless you use Redis or a message broker. If you're deploying on a platform with restrictive firewalls or load balancers that only support HTTP/1.1, gRPC and WebSocket may not work. For a Spring Boot fresher project serving 100 users, REST is the safe default.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using GraphQL for simple CRUD**: Freshers hear GraphQL is modern and add it to a basic user registration API that only needs three endpoints. GraphQL's complexity (schema definition, resolver logic, query parsing) isn't worth it unless you have multiple clients needing different data shapes.
- **Choosing WebSocket for non-real-time data**: Using WebSocket to fetch a user profile on page load adds unnecessary complexity—a single REST GET request is simpler and more cacheable. WebSocket makes sense only when data changes frequently and clients need updates within seconds.
- **Picking gRPC without considering browser clients**: gRPC requires HTTP/2 and doesn't run natively in browsers. If your frontend is React or Angular, you'd need gRPC-Web with an Envoy proxy, adding deployment complexity a fresher project doesn't need.

sections.title: Spring Boot Example
Key Points
content: **REST**: Best for public APIs, simple CRUD, and stateless request-response patterns—works everywhere with minimal setup
**GraphQL**: Solves over-fetching when multiple client types need different data shapes from the same backend schema
**gRPC**: Optimizes for high-throughput internal microservice calls using binary Protocol Buffers instead of JSON text
**WebSocket**: Enables real-time bidirectional communication where servers push data to clients without polling (chat, live feeds)
**Communication pattern**: Choose based on whether you need request-response (REST/GraphQL/gRPC) or streaming (WebSocket)
**Client diversity**: Public third-party clients favor REST, multiple frontend apps favor GraphQL, internal services favor gRPC
**Performance vs simplicity**: gRPC is fastest but complex, REST is slowest but simplest, GraphQL and WebSocket are middle ground

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: I'd choose based on three factors: the communication pattern, who's consuming the API, and performance needs. For most Spring Boot projects serving a mobile or web client, REST is the right starting point because it's simple, stateless, and works everywhere. If I had an iOS app, Android app, and web dashboard all needing different subsets of user data, I'd consider GraphQL to avoid building separate endpoints and letting clients specify exactly what fields they need. That solves the over-fetching problem where mobile clients waste bandwidth downloading data they don't use. For internal microservice calls—like an order service talking to an inventory service thousands of times per second—I'd use gRPC because it's five to ten times faster than REST thanks to binary Protocol Buffers instead of JSON text. The tradeoff is gRPC needs HTTP slash two and doesn't work in browsers without a proxy. For real-time features like a chat app or live stock prices where the server needs to push updates instantly, WebSocket is the only option because it keeps a connection open instead of making the client poll every few seconds. A common mistake freshers make is picking GraphQL or gRPC just because they're modern, without analyzing whether the project actually needs flexible queries or high throughput. Another pitfall is using WebSocket to fetch data on page load—that should just be a REST GET because it's simpler and cacheable. The key is matching the protocol to the access pattern: REST for standard CRUD, GraphQL for flexible client needs, gRPC for speed between services, and WebSocket for real-time push.

beats.text: Choosing an API technology comes down to three questions: who is the client, what is the communication pattern, and what are the performance requirements?

items: REST: browser client, mobile app, public API, standard CRUD — the default; universally supported, easy to debug
GraphQL: multiple clients (web and mobile) needing different data shapes, complex nested data — reduces round trips and payload
gRPC: internal microservice-to-microservice calls where performance matters, streaming needed — binary and fast, not for browsers
WebSocket: real-time bidirectional communication — chat, collaborative editing, live game state — persistent connection
SSE (Server-Sent Events): server pushes updates to browser one-way — live dashboards, notification feeds — simpler than WebSocket

values: Flexible data fetching, multiple client types

beats.text: Default to REST unless you have a specific reason not to. If clients need very different data shapes, consider GraphQL. If you have high-frequency internal service calls, consider gRPC. If the feature requires real-time push from server to client, WebSocket or SSE.
